ui.advisory.title: Before you begin
ui.advisory.body: This experience places you in the first-person perspective of Jesus during the crucifixion. It depicts public execution and includes an intrusive internal-voice system designed to simulate a mind under extreme duress. Physical harm is suggested, never shown in graphic detail, and nothing here uses pain haptics. Every internal voice is artistic interpretation; the Gospels do not record his thoughts. At any moment you can Pause, Exit, turn on Comfort Mode (the internal voices drop to near silence), or step into Witness Mode and stand a few feet away. You can set a ceiling on the internal-voice intensity now and change it at any time.

cue.n_road_quintilian: Romans crucified beside busy roads on purpose. A declamation handed down under Quintilian's name says it plainly: 'Whenever we crucify the guilty, the most crowded roads are chosen, where the most people can look on and be moved by this fear. For every punishment has less to do with the offence than with the example.'
cue.n_road_simon: Mark names the man compelled to carry the cross: Simon of Cyrene, 'the father of Alexander and Rufus', as if his readers knew the sons. Paul greets a Rufus in Rome. In 1941 a tomb of a Cyrenian family was excavated in the Kidron Valley; one ossuary bears the name Alexander, son of Simon. Whether it is the same family cannot be known.
cue.n_wall_pilate: John says the place was 'nigh to the city'. Pilate governed from Caesarea on the coast. In 1961 a reused stone in the theatre there was found to carry his name: Pontius Pilatus, prefect of Judaea. It is the only inscription from his lifetime that names him, and it gives his title in office, prefect, where later writers call him procurator.
cue.n_titulus_custom: Roman writers describe the condemned paraded with a notice of their crime. Suetonius tells of a slave led among banquet guests with a placard giving the reason for his punishment; Cassius Dio, of a man led through the Forum with an inscription declaring why he was to die. The four Gospels agree on the charge written over him, though no two give exactly the same words.
cue.n_soldiers_varus: Crucifixion was no stranger here. After the revolts that followed Herod's death, about thirty-four years before this day, the Roman governor of Syria, Varus, put them down; Josephus records that about two thousand men were crucified. Some of the older people watching on this hill would have remembered it.
cue.n_crowd_tacitus: The Roman historian Tacitus, writing some eighty years later and no friend to Christians, records the execution plainly: 'Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus.' The cross was a Roman penalty, ordered by a Roman governor. Philo of Alexandria, writing in Pilate's own lifetime, preserves a complaint against him: bribery, insults, robbery, and executions without trial.
cue.n_centurion_cicero: To Romans the cross was the death for slaves and rebels, never for citizens. Cicero, prosecuting a corrupt governor, asked: 'To bind a Roman citizen is a crime, to flog him an abomination, to kill him almost parricide: what shall I call crucifying him?' In another speech he said the very word 'cross' should be kept far from a citizen's body, and even from his thoughts, his eyes and his ears.
cue.n_other_lestai: Mark and Matthew call the two men crucified with him lēstai, which the King James Version renders 'thieves'. It is the word Josephus uses for bandits and armed insurgents, and the cross was the penalty Rome kept for rebellion. Luke calls them simply malefactors.
cue.n_sponge_drinks: Two drinks appear in the accounts. Before he was crucified he was offered 'wine mingled with myrrh', and refused it. Proverbs says, 'Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish', and later rabbinic tradition remembers the women of Jerusalem providing such a drink to the condemned as an act of mercy. The vinegar lifted later on a reed was most likely posca, the soldiers' own sour wine.
cue.n_ground_yehohanan: Crucifixion leaves little trace; nails were usually drawn out again. In 1968, in a tomb at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in Jerusalem, an ossuary was found holding the bones of a man named Yehohanan, in his twenties. An iron nail was still lodged in his heel bone, with wood beneath its head. He had been crucified, and afterwards his family laid him in their tomb. One of the very few other examples was found at Fenstanton, in England, and published in 2021.
cue.n_sky_thallus: The darkness was argued over from the start. In the early third century Julius Africanus answered a historian named Thallus, who had explained it as an eclipse of the sun. Africanus objected that no eclipse can happen at Passover, when the moon is full. The oldest manuscripts of Luke say the sun's light failed, with a verb also used of eclipses; later copies read 'the sun was darkened'. The Gospels give the darkness no cause.
cue.n_garden_burial: John says there was a garden here, with a new tomb. Rome often left the crucified on the cross, but Jewish law commanded burial before nightfall: 'his body shall not remain all night upon the tree'. Josephus confirms that the crucified were taken down 'and buried them before the going down of the sun', and Philo had known them handed to their families before a festival. Joseph of Arimathea, a council member who 'had not consented to the counsel and deed of them', asked for the body, and Nicodemus brought about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes.
cue.n_mourners_lament: Not everyone on this road mocked. Luke describes 'a great company of people, and of women, which also bewailed and lamented him', and, at the end, all the people who came together to that sight beating their breasts as they went home. The crowd was never one crowd.
cue.n_women_witnesses: All four Gospels place women at the crucifixion. Matthew, Mark and John name Mary Magdalene among them, with Mary the mother of James and Joses, Salome, and Mary the wife of Clopas. Where a woman's testimony counted for little in law, many historians think the first communities would not have invented women as their principal witnesses.
cue.n_mary_john: Only John places the mother of Jesus at the cross, near enough to be spoken to. Mark and Matthew place the women 'afar off'. The Gospels keep separate memories of this hour; this scene follows John.
cue.c_alexamenos: The earliest known picture of a crucifixion is a mockery. Scratched into plaster on the Palatine Hill in Rome, probably around AD 200, it shows a crucified figure with a donkey's head and a young man raising a hand toward it. The Greek caption reads: 'Alexamenos worships [his] god'.
cue.c_lucian: To educated outsiders the cross was a scandal. In the second century the satirist Lucian mocked Christians for worshipping a man crucified in Palestine. Paul had already written that it was 'unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness'.
cue.c_josephus: Josephus, a Jewish historian writing in Rome around AD 93, mentions Jesus in a passage later embellished by Christian copyists. Most scholars think a core is his own, and in every version it keeps two things: Pilate condemned him to the cross, and 'those that loved him at the first did not forsake him'.
cue.c_psalm22: The cry of abandonment is the first line of the twenty-second Psalm. Many readers note that the psalm does not end there: 'he hath not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted; neither hath he hid his face from him; but when he cried unto him, he heard.'

cue.n_cross_rood: In an Old English poem, The Dream of the Rood, the cross itself speaks, and remembers: 'It was long ago (I remember it still) that I was hewn down at the edge of the forest, cut from my roots.' Then: 'I saw the Lord of mankind hasten with great courage, for he meant to climb upon me. There I did not dare, against the Lord's word, bow or break.' Some of these lines were cut in runes on a stone cross at Ruthwell, thirteen centuries ago. It is a poem, not history.
cue.c_rood: The poem ends its memory of this day in the voice of the wood: 'I trembled when the warrior embraced me. As a rood I was raised; I lifted up a mighty king, the lord of heaven; I dared not bend.'
